title: Part 1, Chapter 23
paragraphs: About what befell Don Quixote in the Sierra Morena, which was one of the rarest adventures related in this veracious history

Seeing himself treated this way, Don Quixote said to his squire, "I've always heard it said, Sancho, that doing good to boors is throwing water into the sea. If I'd believed your words, I'd have avoided this trouble; but it's done now — there's nothing for it but to have patience and take it as a warning for the future."

"Your worship will take warning about as much as I am a Turk," returned Sancho. "But, as you say this mischief might have been avoided if you'd believed me, believe me now, and a still greater one will be avoided. I tell you, chivalry is of no account with the Holy Brotherhood, and they don't care two maravedís for all the knights-errant in the world; and I can tell you I think I hear their arrows whistling past my ears this very minute."

"You're a coward by nature, Sancho," said Don Quixote, "but so you won't say I'm stubborn and never do as you advise, this once I'll take your advice and withdraw out of reach of that fury you dread so much. But on one condition: that never, in life or in death, are you to tell anyone that I retired or withdrew from this danger out of fear, but only in compliance with your entreaties. If you say otherwise you'll be lying; and from this time to that, and from that to this, I give you the lie and say you lie and will lie every time you think it or say it. Don't answer me back; for at the mere thought that I'm withdrawing or retiring from any danger — above all from this one, which does seem to carry some little shadow of fear with it — I'm ready to take my stand here and await alone, not only that Holy Brotherhood you talk of and dread, but the brothers of the twelve tribes of Israel, and the Seven Maccabees, and Castor and Pollux, and all the brothers and brotherhoods in the world."

"Señor," replied Sancho, "to retire is not to flee, and there's no wisdom in waiting when danger outweighs hope. It's the part of wise men to preserve themselves today for tomorrow, and not risk everything in a single day. And let me tell you, though I'm a clown and a boor, I have some notion of what they call safe conduct. So don't repent of having taken my advice; mount Rocinante if you can, and if not, I'll help you; and follow me, for my mother-wit tells me we have more need of legs than hands just now."

Don Quixote mounted without replying, and Sancho, leading the way on his ass, headed for the side of the Sierra Morena, which was close by; Sancho's plan was to cross it entirely and come out at El Viso or Almodóvar del Campo, and hide for some days among its crags to escape the search of the Brotherhood should they come looking. He was encouraged in this by noticing that the stock of provisions carried by the ass had come safe out of the brawl with the galley slaves — something he regarded as a miracle, considering how they pillaged and ransacked everything else.

That night they reached the very heart of the Sierra Morena, where Sancho thought it prudent to spend the night and even some days — at least as many as the supplies he carried might last — and so they encamped between two rocks and among some cork trees. But fatal destiny, which, according to the opinion of those who don't have the light of the true faith, directs, arranges, and settles everything in its own way, so ordered it that Gines de Pasamonte, the famous knave and thief who by Don Quixote's virtue and madness had been released from the chain, driven by fear of the Holy Brotherhood (which he had good reason to dread), resolved to take hiding in the mountains. His fate and fear led him to the same spot to which Don Quixote and Sancho Panza had been led by theirs, just in time to recognise them and leave them to fall asleep. And since the wicked are always ungrateful, and necessity leads to evildoing, and immediate advantage overcomes all considerations of the future, Gines, who was neither grateful nor well-principled, made up his mind to steal Sancho Panza's ass — not bothering about Rocinante, since the horse was a prize good neither to pledge nor sell. While Sancho slept, he stole the ass, and before day dawned he was far out of reach.

Aurora made her appearance, bringing gladness to the earth but sadness to Sancho Panza, for he found that his Dapple was missing; and seeing himself bereft of him, he began the saddest and most doleful lament in the world, so loud that Don Quixote awoke at his cries and heard him saying, "Oh son of my bowels, born in my very house, my children's plaything, my wife's joy, the envy of my neighbours, relief of my burdens, and finally, half-supporter of myself! For with the twenty-six maravedís you earned me daily I met half my charges."

Don Quixote, when he heard the lament and learned the cause, consoled Sancho with the best arguments he could, begging him to be patient and promising to give him a letter of exchange ordering three of the five ass-colts that he had at home to be given to him. Sancho took comfort at this, dried his tears, choked back his sobs, and thanked Don Quixote for the kindness shown him. Don Quixote, for his part, was overjoyed at entering the mountains, since they seemed to him just the place for the adventures he was looking for. They brought back to his memory the marvellous adventures that had befallen knights-errant in similar solitudes and wilds, and he went along reflecting on these things, so absorbed and carried away by them that he had no thought for anything else.

Nor did Sancho have any other care (now that he thought he was travelling in a safe quarter) than to satisfy his appetite with what was left of the clerical spoils; so he marched behind his master loaded with what Dapple used to carry, emptying the sack and packing his paunch — and as long as he could go that way, he wouldn't have given a farthing to meet with another adventure.

While so engaged he raised his eyes and saw that his master had halted and was trying with the tip of his pike to lift some bulky object that lay on the ground. He hurried over to join him and help him if needed, and reached him just as Don Quixote was raising on his pike a saddle-pad with a valise attached to it, half or rather wholly rotten and torn; but they were so heavy that Sancho had to help carry them, and his master directed him to see what the valise contained. Sancho did so with great alacrity; and though the valise was secured by a chain and padlock, from its torn and rotten state he was able to see its contents, which were four shirts of fine holland, and other linen items no less elegant than clean. And in a handkerchief he found a good handful of gold crowns, and as soon as he saw them he exclaimed:
"Blessed be all Heaven for sending us an adventure that's good for something!"

Searching further he found a richly bound little notebook; this Don Quixote asked of him, telling him to take the money and keep it for himself. Sancho kissed his hands for the favour, and cleared the valise of its linen, which he stowed away in the provision sack. Considering the whole matter, Don Quixote remarked:

"It seems to me, Sancho — and it can't possibly be otherwise — that some lost traveller must have crossed this sierra and been attacked and killed by footpads, who brought him to this remote spot to bury him."
"That can't be," answered Sancho, "because if they'd been robbers they wouldn't have left this money."

"You're right," said Don Quixote, "and I can't guess or explain what this may mean; but wait — let's see if there's anything written in this notebook by which we can trace out or discover what we want to know."
He opened it, and the first thing he found in it, written roughly but in a very fine hand, was a sonnet; and reading it aloud so Sancho could hear it, he found it ran as follows:
SONNET

Or Love is lacking in intelligence, Or to the height of cruelty attains, Or else it is my doom to suffer pains Beyond the measure due to my offence. But if Love be a God, it follows thence That he knows all, and certain it remains No God loves cruelty; then who ordains This penance that enthrals while it torments? It were a falsehood, Chloe, thee to name; Such evil with such goodness cannot live; And against Heaven I dare not charge the blame, I only know it is my fate to die. To him who knows not whence his malady A miracle alone a cure can give.
"There's nothing to be learned from that rhyme," said Sancho, "unless by that clew there's in it, one may draw out the ball of the whole matter."
"What clew is there?" said Don Quixote.
"I thought your worship spoke of a clew in it," said Sancho.

"I only said Chloe," replied Don Quixote, "and that no doubt is the name of the lady the author of the sonnet is complaining about; and honestly, he must be a passable poet, or I know little of the craft."
"Then your worship understands rhyming too?"

"And better than you think," replied Don Quixote, "as you'll see when you carry a letter written in verse from beginning to end to my lady Dulcinea del Toboso — for I would have you know, Sancho, that all, or most, of the knights-errant of old were great troubadours and great musicians, both these accomplishments, or rather gifts, being the particular property of lovers-errant. True it is that the verses of the knights of old have more spirit than polish in them."
"Read more, your worship," said Sancho, "and you'll find something that will enlighten us."
Don Quixote turned the page and said, "This is prose, and it seems to be a letter."
"A correspondence letter, señor?"
"From the beginning it seems to be a love letter," replied Don Quixote.
"Then let your worship read it aloud," said Sancho, "because I'm very fond of love matters."
"With all my heart," said Don Quixote, and reading it aloud as Sancho had asked, he found it ran thus:

Your false promise and my sure misfortune are carrying me to a place from which the news of my death will reach your ears before the words of my complaint. You ungrateful one, you've rejected me for one more wealthy, but not more worthy; but if virtue were esteemed wealth, I would neither envy the fortunes of others nor weep for misfortunes of my own. What your beauty raised up, your deeds have laid low; by your beauty I believed you to be an angel, by your deeds I know you are a woman. Peace be with you, who have sent war to me; and Heaven grant that the deceit of your husband be ever hidden from you, so that you don't repent of what you've done, and I don't reap a revenge I would not have.

When he'd finished the letter, Don Quixote said, "There's even less to be gathered from this than from the verses, except that whoever wrote it is some rejected lover." Turning over nearly all the pages of the book, he found more verses and letters, some of which he could read while others he could not; but they were all made up of complaints, laments, misgivings, desires and aversions, favours and rejections, some rapturous, some doleful. While Don Quixote examined the book, Sancho examined the valise, not leaving a corner of it or of the pad that he didn't search, peer into, and explore; not a seam he didn't rip, not a tuft of wool he didn't pick to pieces, lest anything escape for want of care and trouble — so keen was the greed stirred in him by the discovery of the crowns, which came to nearly a hundred. And though he found no more booty, he considered the blanket-tossings, balsam vomitings, stake-blessings, carriers' fisticuffs, missing saddlebags, stolen coat, and all the hunger, thirst, and weariness he had endured in the service of his good master, cheap at the price — since he considered himself more than fully indemnified for it all by the payment he had received in the gift of the treasure-trove.

The Knight of the Rueful Countenance was still very anxious to find out who the owner of the valise could be, gathering from the sonnet and letter, from the gold money and the fineness of the shirts, that he must be some lover of distinction whom the scorn and cruelty of his lady had driven to some desperate course. But in that uninhabited and rugged spot there was no one to be seen of whom he could enquire, so he saw nothing for it but to push on, taking whatever road Rocinante chose — which was wherever he could make his way — firmly persuaded that among these wilds he could not fail to meet some rare adventure. As he went along, occupied with these thoughts, he spotted on the summit of a height that rose before his eyes a man who went springing from rock to rock and from tussock to tussock with marvellous agility. As well as he could make out, the man was nearly unclothed, with a thick black beard, long tangled hair, and bare legs and feet; his thighs were covered by breeches apparently of tawny velvet but so ragged that they showed his skin in several places.

He was bareheaded, and despite the swiftness with which he passed by, as has been described, the Knight of the Rueful Countenance observed and noted all these trifles; though he made the attempt, he was unable to follow him, since it wasn't granted to Rocinante's feebleness to make way over such rough ground, the horse being moreover slow-paced and sluggish by nature. Don Quixote at once concluded that this was the owner of the saddle-pad and of the valise, and made up his mind to go in search of him, even if he had to wander a year in those mountains before finding him. So he directed Sancho to take a shortcut over one side of the mountain, while he himself went by the other, and perhaps by this means they might come across this man who had passed so quickly out of their sight.

"I couldn't do that," said Sancho, "because the moment I separate from your worship fear takes hold of me and assails me with all kinds of panics and fancies. And let what I now say be notice that from this time forward I'm not going to stir a finger's width from your side."

"So be it," said he of the Rueful Countenance, "and I'm very glad you're willing to rely on my courage, which will never fail you, even though the soul in your body fail you. So come on behind me slowly as best you can, and make lanterns of your eyes. Let's make the circuit of this ridge; perhaps we'll come upon this man we saw, who's no doubt the owner of what we found."

To which Sancho answered, "It would be far better not to look for him, because if we find him and he happens to be the owner of the money, it's plain I have to give it back. It would be better, therefore, to take no such needless trouble and instead keep possession of it until in some other less meddlesome and officious way the real owner may be discovered — and perhaps that will be after I've spent it, and then the king will hold me harmless."

"You're wrong there, Sancho," said Don Quixote, "because now that we have a suspicion who the owner is, and have him almost in front of us, we're bound to seek him out and make restitution. And if we don't see him, the strong suspicion we have as to his being the owner makes us as guilty as if he were. So, friend Sancho, don't let our search for him trouble you — for if we find him, it will relieve my mind."

So saying he gave Rocinante the spur, and Sancho followed him on foot and loaded; and after they'd partly made the circuit of the mountain, they found lying in a ravine, dead and half devoured by dogs and pecked by jackdaws, a mule saddled and bridled, all of which further strengthened their suspicion that the man who'd fled was the owner of both the mule and the saddle-pad.

As they stood looking at it they heard a whistle like that of a shepherd watching his flock, and suddenly on their left there appeared a great number of goats, and behind them on the summit of the mountain the goatherd in charge of them, a man advanced in years. Don Quixote called out to him and begged him to come down to where they stood. The goatherd shouted back, asking what had brought them to that spot, seldom or never trodden except by goats or by the wolves and other wild beasts that roamed around. Sancho in return called for him to come down, and they'd explain everything to him.

The goatherd descended, and reaching the place where Don Quixote stood, said, "I'll wager you're looking at that hack mule lying dead in the hollow there, and, faith, it's been lying there now these six months. Tell me, have you come across its master anywhere around here?"
"We've come across nobody," answered Don Quixote, "nor on anything except a saddle-pad and a little valise we found not far from here."

"I found it too," said the goatherd, "but I wouldn't lift it or go near it for fear of some ill-luck or being charged with theft, because the devil is crafty, and things rise up under one's feet to make one fall without knowing why or wherefore."
"That's exactly what I say," said Sancho. "I found it too, and I wouldn't go within a stone's throw of it. I left it there, and there it lies just as it was, for I don't want a dog with a bell."
"Tell me, good man," said Don Quixote, "do you know who the owner of this property is?"

"All I can tell you," said the goatherd, "is that about six months ago, more or less, there arrived at a shepherd's hut some three leagues from here a youth of well-bred appearance and manners, mounted on that same mule lying dead here, and with the same saddle-pad and valise you say you found and didn't touch. He asked us what part of this sierra was the most rugged and remote; we told him it was where we are now, and so in truth it is — for if you push on half a league farther, perhaps you'll not be able to find your way out, and I'm wondering how you've managed to come here, since there's neither road nor path that leads to this spot. Well, on hearing our answer the youth turned about and made for the place we'd pointed out, leaving us all charmed by his good looks and wondering at his question and at the haste with which we saw him depart towards the sierra. After that we saw him no more, until some days later he crossed the path of one of our shepherds, and without saying a word came up to him and gave him several cuffs and kicks, and then turned to the ass with our provisions and took all the bread and cheese it carried; and having done this made off back into the sierra with extraordinary swiftness. When some of us goatherds learned of this, we went in search of him for about two days through the most remote part of this sierra, at the end of which we found him lodged in the hollow of a large, thick cork tree. He came out to meet us very gently, with his clothes now torn and his face so disfigured and burned by the sun that we hardly recognised him; but his clothes, though torn, convinced us, from the recollection we had of them, that he was the person we were looking for. He greeted us courteously, and in a few well-spoken words told us not to wonder at seeing him going about in this guise, since it was binding on him in order to work out a penance imposed on him for his many sins. We asked him to tell us who he was, but we were never able to find out from him; we begged him too, when he was in want of food (which he couldn't do without), to tell us where we could find him, since we would bring it to him with all good will and readiness, and if this wasn't to his taste, at least to come and ask it of us and not take it by force from the shepherds. He thanked us for the offer, begged pardon for the recent assault, and promised in the future to ask for it in God's name without offering violence to anyone. As for a fixed abode, he said he had no other than wherever night might overtake him. His words ended in an outburst of weeping so bitter that we who listened to him must have been stones not to join him in it, comparing what we saw of him the first time with what we saw now. For, as I said, he was a graceful and gracious youth, and his courteous and polished language showed him to be of good birth and courtly breeding; and rustics as we listeners were, even to our rusticity his gentle bearing was enough to make it plain.

"But in the middle of his conversation he stopped and became silent, keeping his eyes fixed on the ground for some time, during which we stood still, waiting anxiously to see what would come of this abstraction; and with no little pity, for from his behaviour — now staring at the ground with fixed gaze and eyes wide open without moving an eyelid, now closing them, compressing his lips and raising his eyebrows — we could see plainly that a fit of madness of some kind had come over him. Before long he showed that what we'd imagined was true, for he arose in a fury from the ground where he'd thrown himself and attacked the first man he found near him with such rage and ferocity that if we hadn't dragged him off, he would have beaten or bitten him to death, all the while crying, 'Oh faithless Fernando, here, here you will pay the penalty for the wrong you've done me; these hands will tear out that heart of yours, the abode and dwelling of all iniquity, but of deceit and fraud above all!' And he added other words, all in effect upbraiding this Fernando and charging him with treachery and faithlessness.

"We forced him to release his hold with no little difficulty, and without another word he left us and rushed off, plunging into these brakes and brambles in such a way that it was impossible for us to follow him. From this we suppose that madness comes upon him from time to time, and that someone called Fernando must have done him a wrong of so grievous a nature that the condition to which it has reduced him bears it out. All this has been since then confirmed on the many occasions on which he has crossed our path — at one time to beg the shepherds to give him some of the food they carry, at another to take it from them by force; for when there's a fit of madness on him, even though the shepherds offer it freely he'll not accept it but snatches it from them with blows; but when he's in his senses he begs it for the love of God, courteously and civilly, and receives it with many thanks and not a few tears. And to tell you the truth, sirs," continued the goatherd, "it was yesterday that we resolved — I and four of the lads, two of them our servants and the other two friends of mine — to go in search of him until we find him; and when we do, to take him, whether by force or with his consent, to the town of Almodóvar, which is eight leagues from here, and there try to cure him (if indeed his malady admits of a cure), or learn when he's in his senses who he is and whether he has relatives we may notify of his misfortune. This, sirs, is all I can say in answer to what you've asked me; and be sure that the owner of the things you found is the man you saw pass by with such nimbleness and so nearly naked."

For Don Quixote had already described how he'd seen the man go bounding along the mountainside, and he was now filled with amazement at what he heard from the goatherd, and more eager than ever to discover who the unhappy madman was. In his heart he resolved, as he'd done before, to search for him all over the mountain, not leaving a corner or cave unexamined until he'd found him. But chance arranged matters better than he expected or hoped, for at that very moment, in a gorge in the mountain that opened where they stood, the youth he wished to find made his appearance, coming along talking to himself in a way that would have been unintelligible up close, much more at a distance. His garb was as described, except that as he drew near, Don Quixote noticed that a tattered doublet he wore was amber-tanned, from which he concluded that one who wore such garments couldn't be of very low rank.

Approaching them, the youth greeted them in a harsh and hoarse voice but with great courtesy. Don Quixote returned his greeting with equal politeness, and dismounting from Rocinante advanced with well-bred bearing and grace to embrace him, and held him for some time close in his arms as if he'd known him for a long time. The other, whom we may call the Ragged One of the Sorry Countenance, as Don Quixote was of the Rueful, after submitting to the embrace pushed him back a little and, placing his hands on Don Quixote's shoulders, stood gazing at him as if trying to see whether he knew him — no less amazed, perhaps, at the sight of the face, figure, and armour of Don Quixote than Don Quixote was at the sight of him. To be brief, the first to speak after the embrace was the Ragged One, and what he said will be told further on.
